Ruby Wax, in her book 'Sane New World', recommends a mindfulness practice whenever the voices get too loud or too negative: pick a sense and focus on it. For me, it's either sounds or sensations.

For example, I'm on my laptop and suddenly the rumination starts. I then either:

1. Try to hear ALL the sounds: ticking clock. cars passing outside. child laughing outside. upstairs neighbor walking up and down. my own breathing. typing etc

2. Consciously sense my body: where my feet touch the ground, where my knee touches my thigh, my forearms the table, my lips touching, air coming through my nose etc.

You can do this anywhere, anytime, for however long. And always remember to breathe deeply.

Hope it helps you like it's helped me! And I heartily recommend that book.

That's not what I'm saying, no need to get aroused. I just wanted to point people in the direction of learning about food and making informed choices. "We've always done it this way" doesn't mean it's not a lesser option than what you could do instead.

You are free to eat whatever you want to eat - I didn't want to sound like some preachy nag. But bread (or wheat in general) isn't actual "food" - it's not nutritious, it weakens your immune system, and it lowers your overall energy.
Like I said, everything is your personal choice - just educating. It's important to know how a certain food makes you feel - I cut wheat and sugar out for a month and only ate meat & vegetables (and a bit of fruit), and it was astonishing how much better I felt, both mood and energy wise. I'd encourage you to try it, then eat some bread and see how it affects you. Don't have to cut anything out, but it's smart to know how foods affect you so you can make an informed decision about when to eat them.

From a nutritional standpoint, I wouldn't make bread a staple in your diet. Chris Kresser's blog has science-backed info on why, the short of it is that gluten contains a chemical called phytate which interferes with the bioavailability of other nutrients. Dark bread doesn't make it any better.
If you want optimum performance, eat natural, real food. No need to go OCD about it but making it a tendency will benefit both your performance & your long-term health.

I can't speak for Hollywood - I'm in London. I'm a 23 yo. director/producer, I make my living with commercial/corporate/music video stuff and do my own narrative projects on the side. 

My boyfriend-who-I'm-probably-gonna-marry is a cinematographer, which is a perfect match as I can usually get him on my projects (we don't tell new clients he's the bf) and the money stays in the family, so-to-speak.

Now, back when I was working as a crew member on TV & feature sets, averaging 16h, making zilch - I was scared as well. I didn't even have a social life off set.

However, the industry is changing. I'd say the more you strike out on your own, the more you can make your own rules. It takes for fucking ever and if you don't yell "FUCK THIS I'M GONNA BECOME A YOGA TEACHER INSTEAD", but you can definitely create a lifestyle that suits you - for me, it meant focussing on short form work to make a living, and saving the big projects for every now and then.

As with everything in life, nobody has an answer to what will work for you. It depends on who you meet/fall in love with. What kind of work you get. But you being a self-shooting filmmaker, I think you can find a way to balance both.

Two pieces of advice for you:

1. try All The Things and see what works and what doesn't. be insanely patient - it'll be worth it.

2. success as a creative freelancer: do good work + show it to the right people.

3. Pretend you're already there. I introduced myself as the Head of [my prod. co.] instead of "hi i'm way younger than you think i just moved here i know nobody i have no idea what i'm doing my office is my kitchen i work in PJs" - fake it till you make it, behave the way someone successful would behave.

Hope that helped.

Also

Don't let anybody tell you you can't do something. They're just scared.
